utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. Registrar, please call the case.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Good afternoon, Your Honour, Case Number IT-04-74-T, the Prosecutor versus Prlic et al.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Today is Monday, the 11 of September, 2006. I would like to greet all those in the courtroom, Mr. Scott and the Defence counsel as well as the accused. We have started one hour late, apparently because of a problem of a logistical nature. Somebody in the chain of command forgot to send the order of transfer of the accused to the Tribunal. Because of this, we've lost one hour of hearing. This of course will have an impact on the time that is left for this hearing. From what I understand, the Prosecution has used 252 minutes. The Defence has used up four hours and 12 minutes up until now. In other words, Mr. Praljak's counsel and all the other counsel who have not spoken yet have six hours left plus possibly one or two additional hours. Today we only have three hours of hearing, so we'll sit until 7.00 p.m. We'll have only one break this afternoon around a quarter to 5.00 and we'll work until 7.00 p.m. As a result, some of the time we've lost will have to be recouped on another day because we will not be able to complete the hearing of the witness. This will not cause any problems to the witness because he works in the building so he will be able to come back at any time. I wanted to turn to the Defence to ask the following question. Last week I asked you if you had any comments about the document P09696 that was disclosed to the Prosecution following an application by the Chamber. I asked the Defence to have a look at the document to see if there were any comments about this document. Mr. Kovacic.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOVACIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, Your Honour, you gave us leave to respond orally on Thursday afternoon. Although the motion was made in writing, we could have responded in writing, but I will be very brief. We oppose the introduction of that evidence. If I may remind Your Honours on the 24th of August, 2004, Witness BK testified under (redacted)

utterances.speaker: MR. KOVACIC
utterances.text: (redacted) "death certificate." This was based on a decision issued by the Prozor public security station 16-15-02-92-94 and the date was the 3rd of April, 1994. The objection was based on the fact that the entry was made pursuant to a document issued by the police rather than a decision issued by a court. Under the valid legislation in Bosnia and Herzegovina, this would be the only legal way of making such an entry into the register of deaths declaring a missing person dead. This is a judicial procedure pursuant to the law. On the 29th of August, the Chamber asked that the Prosecutor tender a judicial decision, these were the very words used, in order to verify the entry into the deaths register. In response to this on the 5th 1 of September, 2006, the OTP delivered the document and asked that a (redacted) 2 (redacted). two documents. The first document is a letter from the chief of the Prozor public security station, the one that was mentioned in the certificate that we saw on the 28th of August before the Court here. I won't repeat the number again. And the Prosecutor -- or rather, this very fact shows that the Prosecutor has not submitted the judicial decision but again a police document. And this was actually the crux of the matter. The letter has an

utterances.speaker: MR. KOVACIC
utterances.text: which such an entry could be made into the register of deaths. On the 24th of August, other death certificates were tendered, and these were actually accompanied by judicial decisions pursuant to procedures to declare a missing person dead, and we did not oppose those documents because these are legally valid documents. We did not insist on seeing on what basis the entries were made, although the Prosecutor was kind enough to show us these. We oppose this exhibit because an entry was made into the register of deaths in an irregular way, which is not legally valid in the system of Bosnia-Herzegovina, and I believe that it would not be valid in most European countries. For this reason, we propose that this exhibit be rejected. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Fine. The Chamber will make a decision about this matter. Let's move -- let's move into private session for a brief period of time.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: [Interpretation] We are in open session, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] All right. Let me now turn to the Defence in order to proceed with the cross-examination of the witness. I don't know who is going to take the floor first.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOVACIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour, the Defence of General Praljak has given its time to the Defence of the accused Dr. Jadranko Prlic so that both times will be used by my colleague.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Excellent news.

utterances.speaker: MS. TOMASEGOVIC TOMIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Your Honours. I only wish to say that the Defence of Mr. Valentin Coric will have questions and most of these will be put by me and then Valentin Coric may put a few questions at the end.

utterances.speaker: MS. TOMASEGOVIC TOMIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Good day, sir, my name is Dijana Tomasegovic Tomic and I am an attorney-at-law acting on behalf of Mr. Coric.

utterances.speaker: WILLIAM TOMLJANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Good afternoon.

utterances.speaker: MS. TOMASEGOVIC TOMIC
utterances.text: I will base most of my cross-examination on your report and the documents already shown to you by the Prosecutor, and I hope that, as you have a very good memory being a historian, I will be able to go through this very quickly because I believe you will be able to remember most of it. At the very beginning before I proceed, I will explain a situation to you, a question of yours to a question previously put to you by my colleague, Ms. Alaburic. She asked you whether the military police, showing the chart with little pictures and the organisational structure, whether the military police was exclusively under the command of the military police administration. And your response was that it was. Do you remember that?

utterances.speaker: WILLIAM TOMLJANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't remember having said it in those words. If I said it with that little qualification, I misspoke or I wasn't careful enough. I should have said that -- I'm not qualified as a non-military expert to say exclusively under whose administration they were, although I know that they did have responsibilities to the military police administration and to the Department of Defence.

utterances.speaker: MS. TOMASEGOVIC TOMIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Could the witness please be shown on e-court document P04262. I know you are not a military expert, but I think this document is very clear so we can clarify matters. This is a document issued by the Main Staff of the HVO. The date is the 17th of August, 1993. Could we scroll down a little so the signature is visible?

utterances.speaker: MS. TOMASEGOVIC TOMIC
utterances.text: It's signed by General Petkovic. I will try to read it for the sake of the record, although I know you can see it. Brigade military police, commanding authority. "It has often occurred that commanders were turning to the chief of the military police concerning the inefficiency of the brigade military police. I hereby warn that the brigade military police is directly subordinate to the brigade commanders. It is part of the brigade formation and has the same status as other units within the brigade." I'll skip over point 2. Point 3 reads: "The chief of the military police can only be asked for professional assistance." 4: "All problems within the brigade police are your problems and should be solved through the command system." Now that we've seen this document, tell me: Did you ever come across the term "brigade military police" in the course of your work?

utterances.speaker: WILLIAM TOMLJANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I have.

utterances.speaker: MS. TOMASEGOVIC TOMIC
utterances.text: And what we have just read out in this document concerning the chain of command, would it correspond to what you discovered in the course of your investigations?

utterances.speaker: WILLIAM TOMLJANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, this corresponds to part of what I've seen in my investigations. I should make very clear at the outset that this particular warning here from General Petkovic deals only with the brigade military police, and that's not all military police. And the other thing I would add is that in other documents that I've seen in other cases, there's a number of people putting forward various theories as to this very issue, although this order from the chief of the General Staff would seem to make this matter clearer, at least from the 17th of August, 1993, onwards.

utterances.speaker: MS. TOMASEGOVIC TOMIC
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Tomljanovich. I will now move on. In your report you say inter alia that the appointment on the 3rd of July, 1993, of --

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Could counsel please give a reference to the interpreters what she's reading?

utterances.speaker: MS. TOMASEGOVIC TOMIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MS. TOMASEGOVIC TOMIC
utterances.text: I will repeat because I don't think the interpreters heard me. In your report you said inter alia in paragraph 97 that the defence department only began to fully function on the 3rd of July, 1992, from the day when Stojic was appointed at its head -- or rather, when the head of the defence department was appointed. Do you remember having said that? Please try to focus now and recall in your memory a report shown to you by the Prosecutor. It's a report on the work of the HVO for 1992. You will tell me whether you remember what I will tell you; and if you don't, we will look at the document. In this way, I hope to save time. In that report inter alia, the tasks of the various HVO bodies are considered. Crime prevention is an area where tasks are defined for the SIS and the Department of Internal Affairs. With respect to SIS it says that a special problem for the SIS in that area was the limited activity of the civilian police or the organs of the MUP, the Ministry of the Interior, as well as the nonfunctioning of the judiciary organs. For this reason, action in certain situations was limited and determined by the above, which had a considerable impact on efficiency in particular instances. In this respect, contacts were established with representatives of the Internal Affairs Department with a view to overcoming the problems that have arisen and the misunderstandings, especially with respect to the competences and powers regarding the sphere of activity of these services. Do you remember this?

utterances.speaker: WILLIAM TOMLJANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, in rough terms this does seem to be very similar to what I've seen, although I should add the caution that whatever is actually in the document is what's the evidence, not my recollection of it. Although, in broad terms, yes, this seems to be -- this seems to be my memory of what was in the 1992 semi-annual report.

utterances.speaker: MS. TOMASEGOVIC TOMIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Could we have P00128 put on e-court, please. The ERN number in B/C/S is 00405085. Would you please look at the last paragraph, I won't read it out loud, where the activities regarding the discovery of organised crime, drug and arms trafficking, and so on is mentioned. You remember that. Could we look at 00405086 ERN number. It's page 9 in the Croatian version.

utterances.speaker: MS. TOMASEGOVIC TOMIC
utterances.text: And please read the second paragraph. That's what I was referring to, and then we can establish with certainty that this is what we're talking about.

utterances.speaker: WILLIAM TOMLJANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: A direct quote: [Interpretation] "A special problem was the very limited activity of the civilian police, i.e., organs of the Ministry of the Interior as well as the non-functioning of the judicial organs. For this reason, action in certain situations was limited and determined by the above which had a considerable impact on efficiency in particular instances. In this respect, contacts were established with representatives of the Department of Internal Affairs with a view to overcoming the problems that have arisen and especially the misunderstandings with respect to the competences and powers regarding the sphere of work of the above- mentioned services."

utterances.speaker: MS. TOMASEGOVIC TOMIC
utterances.text: Thank you very much, Mr. Tomljanovich. For the sake of time, perhaps you could read it to yourself to save time because for me it's sufficient that you tell me that this is it. Now in the same document --

utterances.speaker: MS. TOMASEGOVIC TOMIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Could we see ERN number, because I want you to be sure, 0040596 -- or rather, page 19, paragraph 2.

utterances.speaker: MS. TOMASEGOVIC TOMIC
utterances.text: On this page we have a description of the activities of the Department of Internal Affairs, the civilian police. And inter alia there is a list of what the civil police does. It protects the life and personal safety of people, prevents and discovers criminal offences, traces and arrests the perpetrators of criminal offences, it investigates war crimes and genocide. Is that correct? So previously we established that there was the SIS, Security and Information Service, dealing with crime, but now we also have the civil police in the same period of time. Is this correct?

utterances.speaker: WILLIAM TOMLJANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: [In English] Yes, that's correct, and I recall having cited this passage in my report.

utterances.speaker: MS. TOMASEGOVIC TOMIC
utterances.text: I don't know whether you recall the decree on the organisation and competences of the HVO commissions of 1992?

utterances.speaker: WILLIAM TOMLJANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I do, and I believe I cited that as well.

utterances.speaker: MS. TOMASEGOVIC TOMIC
utterances.text: And in that decree, the Department of the Interior, within the scope of its competences also has a crime detection and forensic work and other kind of work usually done by the crime police as well as traffic control and regulation, checking border crossings. Do you remember that from that decree? If yes, please say so for the record.

utterances.speaker: WILLIAM TOMLJANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I recall that the Ministry of the Interior was given all of the law enforcement duties that would be given to a Ministry of the Interior in most countries.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Considering the nature of your questions that are highly legal in many respects, I'm wondering if you, Witness, as an expert, you reviewed the laws of the former Yugoslavia, laws dealing with investigations. And I wonder if you tried to find out who conducts an investigation when a suspect is -- belongs to the military. Then is the investigation conducted by the civilian police or by the military police? Did you research the matter? Did you review the laws of the former Yugoslavia? I'm now talking about the laws of Bosnia and Herzegovina or Croatia. Did you review the texts in this matter? What can you answer about this?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Well, Your Honour, since your question has two parts I'll answer it in two parts. First of all, for this report I did not make any systematic review of former Yugoslav law, although for various reasons I have looked at laws of SFRJ for various purposes for other research. I didn't look at any laws for interior affairs from the former Yugoslavia for this report. However, in all of my work, not just the work connected with this case but in general, it's always known that standard practice in the former Yugoslavia was that all criminal activity - and I believe it says so in the decrees of the HVO as well - any criminal activity undertaken by military personnel is the responsibility of the military police and not the civilian police because this comes up as an issue very frequently in these cases.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I'm trying to understand what you have said. You are saying that when a crime or misdemeanour is committed within the framework of military activities, in the course of military activities, it's the military police that deals with the investigation, that conducts the investigation, and not the civilian police?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: With misdemeanours, I'm not absolutely positive off the top of my head, although I know with more serious crimes that is the case.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Very well. Do carry on.

utterances.speaker: MS. TOMASEGOVIC TOMIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MS. TOMASEGOVIC TOMIC
utterances.text: Do you remember from this same report on work, the report from 1992, do you remember a part in that report that concerns the Department of Interior Affairs and do you remember mention being made of the fact that due to armed conflict there was more crime committed by people in uniform, there was a rise in the level of crime committed by such individuals? And my other question is: Do you remember that at the time the civilian police was also concerned with crimes committed by men in uniform, by people in uniform? This can be seen in the reports where they mention the number of crimes -- criminal acts committed, the type of crime concerned, the difficulties encountered when dealing with people in uniform who were performing their duties. Do you remember coming across such matters?

utterances.speaker: WILLIAM TOMLJANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, first of all, in connection with the first half of your question, I do recall, not just in this report but in general, reports that crime, both amongst uniformed persons and in general, was increasing during the war. And I've seen that not just in this particular document. The other -- as far as the other question is concerned, I do seem to recall that the civilian police had statistics on the number of person -- crimes committed by persons in uniform, although as far as I know they didn't have any authority to arrest those persons or to process those crimes.

utterances.speaker: MS. TOMASEGOVIC TOMIC
utterances.text: Do you know that the civilian police, the Department of the Interior, kept at least some of the equipment and staff that was part of the former police force, the police force that was in existence before the establishment of the HVO?

utterances.speaker: WILLIAM TOMLJANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't remember having seen that specifically, but I'd be surprised were that not the case.

utterances.speaker: MS. TOMASEGOVIC TOMIC
utterances.text: I'd like to remind you of something contained in your report now, paragraph 117, which states the following. I'll read it out, and it concerns the competence of the civilian police. It says: "The functioning of the civilian and the MUP" -- do you have your report on you? It will be easier for you to follow this passage. Do have a look at paragraph 117.

utterances.speaker: WILLIAM TOMLJANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: [Previous translation continues]... yes, paragraph 117, page 47 in English.

utterances.speaker: MS. TOMASEGOVIC TOMIC
utterances.text: Yes. It says: "The poor functioning of the civilian police and the MUP as well as the judicial system in general was cited as a problem for the HVO military police in September 1992 as well as HVO's military counter-intelligence in the last half of 1992. The Department of Internal Affairs was however able to provide law enforcement to Herceg-Bosna with a 2.580 personnel at their disposal as of the end of 1992." Would I be correct to conclude on the basis of your report that during that period there was an overlapping of the military police's authority, the civilian police's authority, and the SIS's authority, the S- I-S's authority, when it came to cracking down on crime?

utterances.speaker: WILLIAM TOMLJANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, I believe all three of them had responsibilities in regards to crime prevention, although I also think in the various decrees and ordinances what their -- what their spheres of responsibility should have been were fairly clearly outlined, although if an investigation's at the stage where the perpetrator is unknown, then of course the responsibilities of those three agencies could overlap.

utterances.speaker: MS. TOMASEGOVIC TOMIC
utterances.text: Thank you. I'll now go back to the report on the HVO's work from 1992. With regard to the military police during that period of time, the following is stated in the report: In July and in August 1992, the military police was still being established, commands were being established, and it was being linked to the military police administration at the time. Do you remember anything of that sort from the report on the development of the military police?

utterances.speaker: WILLIAM TOMLJANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't remember that specifically being in this report, but once again I would have been very surprised were that not the case at that time. I would have suspected there would be a lot of appointments being made and institutions being set up in this early period.

utterances.speaker: MS. TOMASEGOVIC TOMIC
utterances.text: Do you also remember from that very same report that reference is made to a particular problem of the military police, namely that the military police units did not have the adequate staff to prevent crime. And therefore, attempts were made to cooperate with M-U-P, MUP, bodies in this area. Do you remember this?

utterances.speaker: WILLIAM TOMLJANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, I don't recall if I saw that in this document or other documents, but I do recall repeatedly seeing references to the fact that the military police had a shortage of personnel during most of this period.

utterances.speaker: MS. TOMASEGOVIC TOMIC
utterances.text: And please tell me, is one of the reasons for which the military police didn't have sufficient staff and the fact that many military police units were engaged in military units, they were engaged on the battle- field?

utterances.speaker: WILLIAM TOMLJANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, and you see reports to that effect, particularly in 1993 when fighting is at its worst.

utterances.speaker: MS. TOMASEGOVIC TOMIC
utterances.text: Again I'd like to remind you of that same report which says that it was only in September 1992 that the military police administration was organised through the departments of the general and traffic police and the department for crime prevention. Can you remember this passage or would you like to be shown that part of the report?

utterances.speaker: WILLIAM TOMLJANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, I don't recall that specifically in this report, so if you have a specific question about that on -- yes, it would be good to look at the report; although, if it's a general question, maybe I could answer without it.

utterances.speaker: MS. TOMASEGOVIC TOMIC
utterances.text: No, I'd just like to see whether you could confirm that it was only in September 1992 that the military police administration was organised in the manner I have just mentioned. Since we mentioned up earlier on, organisational matters, et cetera, that's why I'm asking this question. Can you confirm that this actually took place in September? If not, I'll show you the report.

utterances.speaker: WILLIAM TOMLJANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, unfortunately off the top of my head I can't remember the exact date.

utterances.speaker: MS. TOMASEGOVIC TOMIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, I do understand you. Could we see P00128 on the screen, that's the B/C/S version. It's page 11 -- or the ERN is 00405088, that's the ERN number, and we're interested in the second paragraph.

utterances.speaker: MS. TOMASEGOVIC TOMIC
utterances.text: Have a look at the second paragraph, please, and tell me whether that is in fact what I have just been discussing.

utterances.speaker: WILLIAM TOMLJANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. It says here explicitly that over the course of September there was a reorganisation in the military police administration and in the units and that effective on the 1st of October there was a new organisational scheme.

utterances.speaker: MS. TOMASEGOVIC TOMIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you. I'd now like to move on to another subject, which still concerns crime, although I know you're not a military expert --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Before we move on to another subject, there is a question I would like to put to the witness that relates to a document P128. Could we have the following document on the screen -- or, in fact could we see page 23 on the screen, page 23 in the English version, 06618500 is the number. There it is. Sir, could we read out the second paragraph, please?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, I'll read it out in the English. "A new aspect of criminal activity, war crimes and crimes of genocide, has not received due attention because of the war operations in this area. Efforts have been mainly directed to the collecting of data, taking statements from eye-witnesses of crimes. In order to document these criminal offences on-site investigations have been carried out on the sites of mass executions of victims of genocide." And parenthetically here it says in English "sentence as written." "In this sphere, 15 war crimes and crimes of genocide over the civilian population have been registered."

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Very well. This HVO report which covers the entire year 1992 demonstrates that the -- made a list of 15 war crimes or genocide, we don't know what the distinction is, and certain investigations were conducted. Were you familiar with this paragraph and did you ask yourself anything about these 15 war crimes or crimes of genocide? Did you try to delve into the matter?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Well, I did see it and I did find it interesting. Unfortunately I believe this is part of the report of the Ministry of Internal Affairs, and unfortunately if there were any investigations undertaken at this time -- need to remember this is still just for the last half of 1992. If there were any investigations undertaken, I've not seen any documentation directly related to that nor do I know - and I'd be curious to know - what specifically the 15 war crimes are, although given the time period in which they're discussing, I would be extremely surprised were they not discussing crimes committed by Bosnian Serb and JNA forces during that period. Just from the time period from which it's taken you would assume it was in reference to that, but not having seen specifics I can't say that with any certainty.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] There's another question. One of the Judges would like to put.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MINDUA
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Witness, if my memory serves me well, I remember that last time you testified you said that a text have been promulgated with regard to the establishment of military jurisdiction. If that was the case, in the course of your investigations, did you find out anything about these military courts in fact? Did these military courts discover anything about these crimes referred to?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, my colleague's question is very precise. In this paragraph reference is made to crimes committed in the course of combat, in the course of war, and those who are at war are usually members of the military. So the court that would be responsible would be the military court, the military prosecutor, the military police would be responsible for such matters. Did you pose such questions to yourself in order to direct your investigations, if any investigations were in fact conducted?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Well, it did occur to me; however, unfortunately I haven't seen any records from the military courts regarding such matters. I've -- I -- as far as I know, we don't have access or I did not have access to such materials. I understand that perhaps these matters should have been dealt with by the military courts, and the military courts are discussed in my report. But whether or not they did take up these sorts of cases in this period, I don't know from the available documentation.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] There's another question I have on my mind. When an expert is drafting a report and the expert discovers that there is a problem which requires the expert to make an additional effort, shouldn't the expert then ask the person who requested that a report be compiled, shouldn't the expert ask that person to provide him with additional documents? In the light of this paragraph, didn't the idea occur to you to ask the Prosecution to provide you with the files from military courts if he had such files, files that made reference to 15 war crimes or 15 acts of genocide? My -- just a minute, Mr. Scott, the witness will answer the question and then you can take the floor. Yes.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, I was under the impression that I was being given access to everything which was in our possession. Now, the whole question of should we go and make requests and make efforts to find other documentation that the Prosecutor or the ICTY doesn't have physical possession of, that's something we've been working on for years. And generally speaking, in the months and weeks before the report is finished, the prospect of finding anything new from -- based on my own initiative to find something new would be -- the chances of that bearing fruit would be very slim. But it was my understanding that I had access to all the documentation that we had in-house for the purposes of putting this report together.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Very well. Mr. Scott, you wanted to take the floor.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: Just to point out, Your Honour, as I did last week on several occasions. This was beyond the scope of the report. Mr. Tomljanovich was never commissioned to conduct a detailed inquiry into the workings of the military courts or an investigation of specific cases. Only a broad generally overview of the governmental and political structures. So he was never asked, it was never part of his job to look at that. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Mr. President, I may be off, but I do recall the gentleman saying something to the effect that there were others in the office of the Office of the Prosecution that were dealing with court documents. Perhaps the witness could verify whether my memory serves me correctly. Secondly, in light of your questioning, perhaps you could ask the gentleman if he made any efforts, specific efforts in the field to go to the municipalities, to go to the -- to get these records. I understand he says he didn't come across any, but did he actually make an effort? Because he's claiming no fruit would be borne by efforts. What efforts were made by the gentleman?

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: He was never asked to do it, Your Honour. He was never asked to do it, Your Honour. I think the point has been made.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. Karnavas, Mr. Scott has provided the response. The witness was never asked to make this effort, and as a result the witness didn't think it was necessary to pursue the matter to ask his colleagues in the OTP whether they had such documents or to go to the relevant sites themselves to look for such documents, that wasn't part of the task assigned to the witness. Yes, Mr. Karnavas.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Getting back to what I stated earlier, I believe it was on -- somewhere between -- I believe it's 6230, page 6230, lines 21 to approximately 632 -- 6231, line -- line 4, where the gentleman indicated that other - "other persons who I know from my office have looked at those materials," meaning materials from courts. I'm just mentioning that to just verify that my memory was indeed, you know, rather accurate.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, you have understood the purpose of the question, even if this wasn't, strictly speaking, the task assigned to you, did you discuss this matter with your colleagues from the Office of the Prosecutor? Because you said that there are other individuals from the OTP who had documents. This was page 6230, is this something you looked into or not because it wasn't part of your task?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: No, this was something I looked into. Late in the drafting of my report when I had a fairly final draft put together, I did ask the lawyers responsible for different parts of the case which were affected by this report if they'd thought I missed anything particularly important. I did get suggestions of about -- gosh, maybe about a dozen things to look into. Now, of the things that were recommended to me, some of them were not included in the report just because the problem with the report -- and it's in evidence here and elsewhere, for -- thank you. In general, the problem always is with a report of this sort, I could go into a great deal of detail on any one of these subjects, and fortunately or unfortunately we have a great deal of documentation at the lower level for many of these problems which are mentioned in the report. The question is always with something that's intended to be an overview of the structures broadly speaking and intended to assist the Judges in understanding those structures and processes in a global sense, the question is always how much local detail is appropriate. And that's something which is a judgement call on my part. Certainly if I had gone into details with every document which was available for every particular office and every particular municipality, we'd have a much longer document in front of us.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. Karnavas, perhaps we should stop there.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: If I could -- if I may, Your Honour, because I believe at the commencement of the cross-examination, Mr. Murphy indicated -- had a certain request with respect to communication between the gentleman and Office of the Prosecution. In his answer he's now just admitted that during the drafts this OTP employee, who's a member of the Prosecution team, asked that the drafts be looked at and what if anything he missed so they could put in -- obviously into his report. In light of that admission, I do -- I would like to renew now, renew the request made by Mr. Murphy and I would like for the gentleman concretely to tell us what if anything he was told was missing so he could put it in so he could dovetail the Prosecution's theory and its indictment. And also, I would like all communications between this gentleman and the members of the team with respect to the writing of this particular report because it seems to have taken a life of its own.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: Your Honour, our position remains the same as it was before. Nothing has changed. Absolutely nothing has changed since the witness first began testifying. In fact, I indicated just a moment ago that in very clear terms these were not matters of which he was commissioned to conduct this work. There's further reason there's no basis for any inquiry into any of this at all, and we continue to maintain our position. We object to any such production under Rule 70. We think it's not appropriate.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE TRECHSEL
utterances.text: Mr. Tomljanovich, did you write anything into this report because members of the Prosecution team told you you must write this in the report?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: No one told me I must put anything into the report. My question was: Have I forgotten anything? And is there anything, broadly speaking, that should be addressed here that I don't know about because of the limitations of my own knowledge that should be addressed here where appropriate. I was told -- the only instance -- very little -- I got very little feedback in that regard. I was surprised I didn't get more. What I was told amongst other things was that I could not include more specific documentation in regards to specifics on some of these issues. I then asked: Well, wasn't the point of my report to be at a higher level and not so specific? And I was told: No, in these particular instances -- because the thing I was very worried about over the whole course of the report is overlapping with evidence -- other witness's evidence, which is something which would be very easy to do. So I had thought that certain areas would be covered by other witnesses, but in two small areas I was told that it would not. And so I did write on those subjects, although I did not include all the documents which were suggested to me because I did not think all of them were appropriate for a report at this level and of this length.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE TRECHSEL
utterances.text: So can I understand you as saying that it was you and not anyone from the Prosecutor's office who finally decided what you put or did not put into the report?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, absolutely. And I don't believe anyone saw my final draft until it was disclosed. I don't think anyone read through it beginning to end, other than myself. And one intern I had proofreading my English and punctuation.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE TRECHSEL
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Fine. We'll move on to something else, but having listened to this exchange, apparently what I understand is that you asked the Prosecutor or one of -- some of your colleagues, you said: This is the first draft of my report. Can I add anything else to it? And then you said that to your great surprise you were told that it was excellent, that there was no need to inquire about other subjects. Is that the way we should understand your answer?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, and I should add that at the same time earlier on in the drafting of this report, I was also told by a number of people who'd looked at it: Well, this will be covered by other witnesses and you don't need to go into great detail about, you know, matters which will be dealt with in, say, the presidential transcript that will be dealt with by other witnesses, so I didn't need to worry about those things. But my motivation in asking was to see if there were any major issues or any major funds of documents which I'd missed and with a few small exceptions I had not missed anything, but I wanted to make sure I had not.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Fine. So you've given us a very specific answer. Mr. Murphy.

utterances.speaker: MR. MURPHY
utterances.text: Well, Your Honour, it is specific, but it raises the question again as I think Judge Trechsel's questions did as to whether we're dealing here with an expert report or a coordinated piece of advocacy prepared by the Office of the Prosecutor as a whole. And this is the entire problem here as having someone who has played -- has been so intimately connected with the preparation and investigation of the case in posing as an expert before this Trial Chamber. This is exactly the sort of problems we discussed. Your Honour, I renew my objection to the admissibility of this report, and indeed I renew my request, as Mr. Karnavas did on my behalf, for access to whatever input other members of the team had to this document.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] We take note of your remarks. You're raising again an issue that has already been debated, and because of this Mr. Scott has to take the floor again.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: Only to say, Your Honour, that I submit that the state of the record now is stronger than ever, stronger than it ever was that this has been a fully independent report by Mr. Tomljanovich, that he controlled the content of the report. The only thing he has talked about this afternoon was requesting whether certain collections of information had -- other collections should be considered. But the state of the record now is stronger than ever that this was an independent report prepared by Mr. Tomljanovich.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. Kovacic.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOVACIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour, I wish to formally join with the Prlic Defence with respect to the request that the OTP urgently disclose to us all the internal correspondence with the expert, especially from the time when his first draft of the report was circulated. It is not just the issue raised by my colleague Mr. Murphy, that is the closeness of the link between the expert and the OTP, it's that these notes could be used as evidence, that the Office of the Prosecutor actively participated or may have actively participated in the preparation of this report, even through their critique of it. And that is why I reiterate the request that this correspondence be disclosed to us. It would clarify many things.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Fine. The Chamber has already ruled on the matter. I don't see any reason for us to reconsider the issue. You can proceed, Madam.

utterances.speaker: MS. TOMASEGOVIC TOMIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Your Honour. I know that this discussion was useful, but it has taken a lot of time from the Defence of Mr. Coric, so that when a count is made of the time we used, could these 20 minutes be subtracted from my time, please?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Do not worry. You will have these additional 20 minutes.

utterances.speaker: MS. TOMASEGOVIC TOMIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MS. TOMASEGOVIC TOMIC
utterances.text: I wanted to go back after His Honour Judge Antonetti showed to you this chapter concerning war crimes, you said that you assumed it was part of a report referring to the work of the department Of Internal Affairs, the MUP, but you weren't sure as far as I can recall?

utterances.speaker: WILLIAM TOMLJANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, I assume it is but I'm not sure because I can't page backwards on the electronic copy to be sure which chapter it's in. I can only read this one part here on the screen.

utterances.speaker: MS. TOMASEGOVIC TOMIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Could the part beginning with B be shown to the witness? It's page 18 in the B/C/S, 00405095, and the title is B, internal affairs.

utterances.speaker: MS. TOMASEGOVIC TOMIC
utterances.text: And a concluding question about the topic raised by His Honour. In view of the fact that this paragraph is in the part of the report relating to internal affairs, may one conclude that it is the department of internal affairs that dealt with investigating this kind of crime?

utterances.speaker: WILLIAM TOMLJANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, certainly they must have at this time and in these instances, that doesn't necessarily mean that at other times and other instances other persons would not have been involved as well, because this is prior to the founding of the War Crimes Commission, I think, that we discussed earlier in my testimony.

utterances.speaker: MS. TOMASEGOVIC TOMIC
utterances.text: Thank you. I would now like to move on, and our text topic will have to do with military justice department, the military courts and the military prosecutor's offices. Although you're not a military expert, it's usually the military police, after carrying out an investigation, that sends a written report to the military prosecutor's office, and then the military prosecutor institutes proceedings before military courts in cases where the system is functioning normally. Is that correct?

utterances.speaker: WILLIAM TOMLJANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. If things get that far, that's the normal chain of events with an investigation in the military.

utterances.speaker: MS. TOMASEGOVIC TOMIC
utterances.text: In your report you mention this, and I believe you will recall that it was only on the 17th of October, 1992, that the HVO issued a decree about district military courts and a decree about district prosecutor's offices establishing these military courts and prosecutor's offices. Do you recall that?

utterances.speaker: WILLIAM TOMLJANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I recall that. I also recall the 3rd of July decree on courts in general, but I recall this as well, yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. TOMASEGOVIC TOMIC
utterances.text: I'm asking you now only about military courts, and that was the 17th of October, 1992, the date of the decree establishing them.

utterances.speaker: WILLIAM TOMLJANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. TOMASEGOVIC TOMIC
utterances.text: May one conclude from this that the military courts and military prosecutor's offices did not in fact exist before the 17th of October, 1992, and after the establishment of the HVO, even on paper?

utterances.speaker: WILLIAM TOMLJANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, certainly not on paper at this level. Whether or not people were organising things locally, I can't say with any certainty. But at this level, that's correct, not until the 17th of October.

utterances.speaker: MS. TOMASEGOVIC TOMIC
utterances.text: Tell me, please, in your report, if I interpret it correctly and I believe I did, more than once you refer to particular documents and reports from which it transpires that the military justice system in fact was not functioning until the end of 1992 in a normal way.

utterances.speaker: WILLIAM TOMLJANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, it --

utterances.speaker: MS. TOMASEGOVIC TOMIC
utterances.text: Do you recall that from your report?

utterances.speaker: WILLIAM TOMLJANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, it's mentioned in the document we're looking at and it's also mentioned in the minutes of the meetings of the HVO, HZ-HB around this time, end of 1992, beginning of 1993.

utterances.speaker: MS. TOMASEGOVIC TOMIC
utterances.text: Do you recall from your report the part where you speak of the competences of the military courts, where you say that they were authorised to carry out proceedings against military personnel but also civilians if they violated a military institution?

utterances.speaker: WILLIAM TOMLJANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I do recall that -- or if they violated military statutes, I think not violated a military institution. There might be a trouble with the translation there.

utterances.speaker: MS. TOMASEGOVIC TOMIC
utterances.text: Do you recall from that same decree concerning district military courts who was authorised to institute criminal proceedings, to submit a criminal report, to carry out a police investigation in proceedings before military courts?

utterances.speaker: WILLIAM TOMLJANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Proceedings would be initiated by the military police, and then I believe carried out by the district military prosecutors. That's my recollection from the top of my head.

utterances.speaker: MS. TOMASEGOVIC TOMIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Could we have on e-court document P00592. That is the decree on district military courts, and could we look at Article 27, please. Article 27, please. If we can open it.

utterances.speaker: MS. TOMASEGOVIC TOMIC
utterances.text: I will read the first paragraph to you which says: "The commander of a military unit and a military institution is duty-bound to take all necessary measures to prevent the perpetrator of a crime, under official prosecution, from hiding or escaping, and must attempt to preserve all the traces of the criminal act and all objects that may serve as evidence. He must also obtain all information relevant to the criminal proceedings." "It is the duty of the commander of a military unit or institution to inform the district military prosecutor or his superior commander immediately of any information mentioned in paragraph 1 of this article." Now that you've read this passage, would you agree with me if I were to say that the powers I asked you about previously under this decree do not belong to the military police with respect to all military personnel, but it is the commanders of each unit that have these powers with respect to the members of their units. Am I right in saying this?

utterances.speaker: WILLIAM TOMLJANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, I would say that this article here is intended to list the duties of individual military commanders in the field, and it lists them in the first paragraph. And in the second paragraph it gives them the duty to inform the district military prosecutor of such things. Now, what that might say about other instances which do not directly involve a military -- do not involve the intervention of a military commander I couldn't say from this article. But from this article, yes, he's got a direct -- the military commander has a direct duty to inform the district military prosecutor of these particular things here.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE TRECHSEL
utterances.text: If I may just as a matter of precision, are you saying that this is a competence which is not, according to the text before us, an exclusive competence?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I don't see anything here and I hadn't thought of it before, but I don't see anything in this article which would lead me to believe it is exclusive necessarily.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE TRECHSEL
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Which doesn't mean that it isn't necessarily, but I don't see anything that indicates that.

utterances.speaker: MS. TOMASEGOVIC TOMIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MS. TOMASEGOVIC TOMIC
utterances.text: Tell us, please, in view of the fact that you've studied this decree, did you find an article in it regulating the duties of the military police towards the military court and the military prosecutor? Did you find such an article? And if you did, could you tell us which article it is? Since you didn't deal with it in your report; that's why I'm asking you.

utterances.speaker: WILLIAM TOMLJANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Off the top of my head, I can't say this is a relatively long article -- or relatively long decree with many articles. Off the top of my head, I can't say whether or not the specific duties of the military police are anywhere in this.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. Kovacic.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOVACIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour, I hesitate to interrupt, but someone may have misread something here. Perhaps it might be better to clarify it now than to have to come back to it later. The article before Article 27, the one we've been discussing - and it's quite clear from the text - speaks quite explicitly about the authority of a military commander or a military member to detain someone so that this select-specific tells us who has the right to detain a perpetrator. The witness is reading this provision as if it relates to initiating proceedings; that's not what is being dealt with here. And this was discussed on the previous page as well. That's my understanding, but I only wish to contribute to clarifying this article.

utterances.speaker: MS. TOMASEGOVIC TOMIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I disagree with my colleague Mr. Kovacic because I think that this article in a summary fashion regulates several stages in the proceedings ending in arrest and detention. But as Mr. Tomljanovich himself has said that he is not a legal expert, there will be a time for us to analyse this with a witness who will be a legal expert and who will be able to explain what this article is about. I just wish to say that it's quite telling, that's why I read the first paragraph, that there is a clear list of the duties of a commander to preserve traces or evidence, to inform the prosecutor, to prevent a person from escaping. This is not necessarily linked solely to detention.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Sir, apparently you're not the appropriate expert to deal with questions of a military nature, but in Article 27 we have this provision about the commander of a military unit. Is that the commander of a brigade or the commander of a unit positioned on the ground? There might be an officer with three soldiers, and in that configuration, is the officer with these three soldiers, is he the one who is supposed to take action or is he supposed to report the matter to his superior commander for the commander of the brigade to report the matter to the military prosecutor? If you can answer this question, please answer; if it's too complicated, just tell us that this does not come within your domain of expertise.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Well, it doesn't necessarily come within my expertise, although I can explain a few things that might make it clearer, although I'm not sure that I can explain all aspects of your question. One problem with B/C/S as opposed to, say, French or English is that there's no such thing as a definite article or an indefinite article that would say "a" or "the" the translator's assumption that puts it there or does not put it there. However, my reading, if you look at the second paragraph in Article 27, since it says that a commander of a unit or institution, I would imagine that means any commander, a commander, as opposed to the brigade commander. That, I think, sheds some light on the first half of the question. It is my understanding then, which is not definitive, that this would refer to any commanders, not just brigade commanders. Since it's not specified and since they say here in one instance: "Commanders of units or institutions."

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] In other words, when you're saying that it's -- it applies to any commander, it applies to all the officers? Is that what you're saying?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: That's how I would read it. I would read this as being binding on any commander of a military unit or institution.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE TRECHSEL
utterances.text: Witness, I put it to you that a military unit is a relatively well-defined and general notion which in other languages is called a company. That's a minimum, minimum size which -- which is regarded as an essential entity. A commander is not someone below a lieutenant who has just a platoon or even a corporal, a non-commissioned officer, even less is not a commander. A staff officer in a battalion regiment and so forth is not a commander. The commander is the chief of at least a company. But a brigade commander is a commander, a battalion commander is also a commander. Would you disagree with that?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Well, I don't -- I don't know enough to disagree with that or agree with that. Apparently Your Honour knows a great deal more about this than I do, and not being an expert in military affairs I don't know if the term "commander" would only apply to -- I guess what you're saying is captains and above if they have a specific unit to command.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE TRECHSEL
utterances.text: I wish to stress that I am not a military expert either.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yeah.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Just one more question. I do not remember, but tell us, yourself, did you do your military service in the United States?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: No, I did not. I spent three years in a military high school which I didn't finish, and that's the extent of my military -- that's the extent of my military experience.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: During this pause, Your Honour, if I may, I'm getting a little nervous about the line of the questioning, particularly from the Bench because it's quite obvious that the gentleman is not competent in this particular field. And I draw the attention to the -- the first question posed by Judge Trechsel as to -- asking the gentleman to give his opinion with respect to exclusivity. And the gentleman, knowing that he's not an expert, knowing that he doesn't know how to read the law, by his own admission from last week, nonetheless went ahead and speculated. I am rather troubled, and I note this on the record because I saw Judge Trechsel taking notes, and I speak very frankly, I am worried that at some point we are going to accredit more than we should to this gentleman's testimony. I think it's okay to speculate, but we're wasting our time asking questions of this -- such technical nature to such someone as this gentleman who obviously -- simply does not have the background or the experience to answer these sorts of questions, and by his own admission is not here to do so.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE TRECHSEL
utterances.text: I hope you noted, Mr. Karnavas, that I took note also of your sorrow and worries.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: I did, I did. And please keep doing that, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE TRECHSEL
utterances.text: I do.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Very well. Please proceed. We have five minutes left before the break.

utterances.speaker: MS. TOMASEGOVIC TOMIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MS. TOMASEGOVIC TOMIC
utterances.text: Mr. Tomljanovich, just a brief text from your report which I wish to analyse because it seems to me there may be a mistranslation. It's paragraph 129 which in the Croatian version says: "Stojic," that's line 4, "claimed that the military courts were still not functioning, saying that there were over 1.000 military police complaints which had still not been processed by the courts." Now, what bothers me here is complaints or tuzbena ibasterij [phoen]. In the original it says "reports" and that is a significant difference. I only wish to establish whether you would agree with me that the B/C/S word prijava, as in criminal report, would be the correct translation of this into B/C/S?

utterances.speaker: WILLIAM TOMLJANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: The correct translation of which English word? Complaint?

utterances.speaker: MS. TOMASEGOVIC TOMIC
utterances.text: [In English] Complaint.

utterances.speaker: WILLIAM TOMLJANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, and it's a legal police term of art, yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. TOMASEGOVIC TOMIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you. I would now like to move on to disciplinary responsibility. To the best of your recollection, who -- whose duty was it to establish disciplinary responsibility and carry out disciplinary proceedings? Do you remember or should I show you the document?

utterances.speaker: WILLIAM TOMLJANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Off the top of my head, I think the decree on military discipline from July 1992 lists the commanders themselves as responsible.

utterances.speaker: MS. TOMASEGOVIC TOMIC
utterances.text: Let's just establish this and put on e-court document P00293, Article 19. I'll begin reading and then you can check. In Article 19 it says: "Superior officers shall establish the disciplinary responsibility of their subordinates according to the prescribed procedure and shall pronounce disciplinary measures for which they are authorised hereby." Would you now say that you recall that it is the superior officers who are authorised?

utterances.speaker: WILLIAM TOMLJANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, that's exactly what it says here in the first part of Article 19.

utterances.speaker: MS. TOMASEGOVIC TOMIC
utterances.text: Now that we're here, could we have a look at Article 29? I'll start reading it again. It says: "When an authorised officer assesses that a violation of military discipline also constitutes a criminal offence, this shall be handed over through the regular procedure to the competent prosecutor." I won't read any further. Does it follow from this that when a criminal offence has been committed simultaneously as a breach of military discipline, it is again the superior officer who is competent to establish responsibility? Am I right? I'm not sure I'd use that wording. If it's also a punishable act and not merely a disciplinary act, my reading of this is that it will be handed over to the official prosecutor and he will deal with the criminal problems. Insofar as it is a disciplinary problem, which will be at a lower -- lower level of seriousness, that would be taken care of by the commander.

utterances.speaker: MS. TOMASEGOVIC TOMIC
utterances.text: Yes, but the authorised officer is the person who forwards the case to the authorised prosecutor in cases of criminal offences?

utterances.speaker: WILLIAM TOMLJANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, it doesn't necessarily say "in all cases." It just says that if a disciplinary violation represents something serious enough to be a punishable act, then the superior officer should transfer it on to the proper authorities, which I take to mean the military prosecutor.

utterances.speaker: MS. TOMASEGOVIC TOMIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, that was my question. That's fine.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Ms. Alaburic.

utterances.speaker: MS. ALABURIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Your Honour. Perhaps we could clarify a minor matter. There are two ways in which disciplinary rules can be violated. There are disciplinary errors and there are disciplinary violations. My colleague's question concerns disciplinary errors, and the witness keeps talking about disciplinary violations, which is quite a different matter regulated by -- it falls under paragraph 3, Article 51 and onwards. I just wanted to avoid us confusing these two separate terms, these two separate concepts.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Very well. I'll summarise the problem because we have to have a break now. Article 29 seems to say that when an officer is familiar with an act that could require disciplinary measures and that it could be punishable, in such a case he has to refer the matter to the Prosecutor. Is that your reading of this article?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, if it's something that is of that nature, that's what he should do, he should forward this matter on to the responsible authorities or to the authorities who have that duty.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Very well, that seems clear to me.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE TRECHSEL
utterances.text: I must confess that I did not at all understand the question of Madam Alaburic as to two types of disciplinary violations. Maybe after the break I would need some clarification. There is a plurality here I think of semi-medical -- semi-military experts and this doesn't necessarily make it easier. Perhaps we would close the chapter of these military special questions and wait for a real military expert to be brought before us. We can think about this in the break.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, it's ten to 5.00. The registrar has just told me that for technical reasons it's necessary to have a half an hour break. So we will resume at 5.20 exactly.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] It's 5.20 and we'll be working until 7.00 p.m.

utterances.speaker: MS. TOMASEGOVIC TOMIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Your Honour. Could we now see document P04699 on the screen. It's a report on the HVO's work from the -- for the period from January to June. In the B/C/S version -- could we first have a look at page 18 in the B/C/S version. 00563781 is the number for the English translation, and we're interested in page 11.

utterances.speaker: MS. TOMASEGOVIC TOMIC
utterances.text: While we're waiting for the document to appear I'll move on. I don't think it says that it's a report for the HVO's work for the period January to June 1993. I don't think that's been recorded in the transcript. I'm interested in the third paragraph in the B/C/S version, page 11 in the English version. I see that we haven't got that page on the screen yet, but I'll read out the third paragraph. It's page 18 in the B/C/S version, and page 11 in the English version. In paragraph 3 it says -- well, mention is made to SIS's activities. It says: "At the same time the service registered -- recorded a number of criminal activities, theft, smuggling, rape, the misappropriation of vehicles, and other crimes. Crimes which were committed by HVO members, by members of the military, and by civilians, and these crimes were committed in the territory of Central Bosnia, Travnik, Vitez, and Bugojno, as well as in the territory of Mostar and other municipalities." My question is whether one can draw the conclusion from the text that we have just read out that the SIS was also involved in work that concerned crime prevention, they were involved in crime prevention when people in uniform were at stake, not necessarily the active military forces.

utterances.speaker: WILLIAM TOMLJANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. In general it was the job of the SIS to keep an eye on the military, as military counter-intelligence for any misbehaviour or trouble within the military or any outside forces working within the military. And criminal problems of soldiers would be involved within the area they were looking into.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE TRECHSEL
utterances.text: Excuse me, could you indicate in the English version the paragraph you have been quoting because on page 11 there is a paragraph that starts with the words "at the same time" but it doesn't follow at all as you have read.

utterances.speaker: MS. TOMASEGOVIC TOMIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Just a minute, Your Honour. I'll do so immediately. It's the last paragraph on page 11, and it continues on the following page, page 12. And also the paragraph after that one. I'll tell you the exact order now -- yes, it's in the middle. I apologise. Perhaps I wasn't precise enough.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE TRECHSEL
utterances.text: Thank you. But I like your yellow numbers, that was very helpful. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MS. TOMASEGOVIC TOMIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Let's see page 20 in the B/C/S version of the same document and in the English version it would be page 13. In the B/C/S version it's the fourth paragraph, in the middle of the page. And in the English version you can also see the paragraph that starts with the words: "The department for crime prevention." We're now talking about the military police for the same period of time. It says: "The crime prevention unit in the military police administration has been transformed in that its authority has been delegated to the level of the operative zone, has been transferred to that level."

utterances.speaker: MS. TOMASEGOVIC TOMIC
utterances.text: My question is as follows: On the basis of this text, can we conclude that during that period of time the responsibility for preventing crime had been taken over by military police units within operative zones and that therefore the bodies that have authority -- that had authority in those zones were responsible for that matter -- for such matters and not the military police administration?

utterances.speaker: WILLIAM TOMLJANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, what you're asking there, the control over military police who are inside the various operative zones is a matter which has been litigated at great length in a number of different trials here. I don't know what, if any, definitive answer has been made as to this question. Although, this particular section here and in all of the HVO's reports, the various sections reporting on themselves are responsible for writing these things up. The military police administration here has indicated that they're moving the powers of crime prevention down to the operative zone level. So that's, I think, one piece of evidence which contributes to a conclusion regarding that problem. But the whole problem of control of military police is an extremely complicated problem, which unfortunately I don't feel qualified to make any firm conclusions on.

utterances.speaker: MS. TOMASEGOVIC TOMIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you. Could we now see document P09551 on the screen. It's a report from the defence department for the period July to December 1993. So the ERN number is 00405197, that's for the B/C/S version. Unfortunately I don't know the number for the English version. Of course we seem to have a problem with the translation, but I can read it out and Mr. Tomljanovich can follow the text. The ERN number in the B/C/S version is 0040 -- yes, that's the right page. Could we have a look at the last paragraph, the last paragraph and the penultimate one. I'll read the text out now, the part that I'm interested in. It says: "On the basis of the situation in military police units and in the military police administration, the course of December 1993 commenced to establish a new HVO military police as of the 1st of December, 1993. This new body came into existence as of the 1st of December." Then it says: "This new structure of the military police means that the system of commanding the military police units has been changed so that all military police units are under the command of the military police administration and in the course of their daily duties the military police shall be subordinated to HVO commanders."

utterances.speaker: MS. TOMASEGOVIC TOMIC
utterances.text: Does what I have just read out confirm my previous conclusion, the conclusion I drew with regard to the previous document?

utterances.speaker: WILLIAM TOMLJANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I -- just one correction, though, I think there's a mistake in the transcript. When you read out the text of this the first reference to a month said that over the course of December 1993, and in the original, the month is Studeni, which would be November.

utterances.speaker: MS. TOMASEGOVIC TOMIC
utterances.text: Yes, November, that's correct.

utterances.speaker: WILLIAM TOMLJANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: This indicates that in -- at least of November -- well, from the beginning of December 1993, the military police were re-formed into different units. And as part of this, from that date onwards, they were to be responsible in their day-to-day workings to the HVO commanders, from that point onward.

utterances.speaker: MS. TOMASEGOVIC TOMIC
utterances.text: I'll now have to analyse this though. It says: "This new structure of command and control in the military police has been changed so that all military police units are now under the command of the military police administration." I think the military police administration also had command over all military police units before this, so would it be necessary to say a change was at stake? Or if that had been the case, if the military police had been in charge of them, it wouldn't be necessary to say a change was at stake?

utterances.speaker: WILLIAM TOMLJANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Although, and I'm having trouble reading the original here because it's very small -- the changes could be in reference to reforming and creating the light assault battalions and not - let me see -- not necessarily in regards to whom they are responsible. Let's see here.

utterances.speaker: MS. TOMASEGOVIC TOMIC
utterances.text: Mr. Tomljanovich, the text is more legible. It says: "The new structure means that the system of command and control has also been changed." Can you see that part? That's what I'm trying to draw your attention to.

utterances.speaker: WILLIAM TOMLJANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: It says that the -- I see that the -- the way in which they are commanded has been changed and in their daily function -- carrying out of their duties from -- within their sphere of responsibility of the military police, they're subordinate to the commanders of -- individual commanders of the HVO, which implies implicitly that that had not been the case before but not explicitly.

utterances.speaker: MS. TOMASEGOVIC TOMIC
utterances.text: That -- you've avoided answering my question again. Maybe I wasn't clear enough. I'm interested in the part that says the bodies being structured -- changed in such a way that the military police administration will be in command of all military police units. If we follow your reasoning, then this means that the military police administration wasn't in command of all those units until this new structure was established.

utterances.speaker: WILLIAM TOMLJANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, I don't believe that I would say that. Looking at this again they say that under the new system for the daily carrying out of their duties, the military police units are subordinated to unit commanders of the HVO.

utterances.speaker: MS. TOMASEGOVIC TOMIC
utterances.text: Please, read out the first two lines of that paragraph again.

utterances.speaker: WILLIAM TOMLJANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yeah, with the new structure, so that meaning from December 1st, 1993, onwards.

utterances.speaker: MS. TOMASEGOVIC TOMIC
utterances.text: And then it says: "The system of command and control over the military police units has been changed so that all military police units are now under the command of the military police administration." In my opinion, if the military police administration had been in command of all units before this period of time, it wouldn't have been necessary to write this sentence. Do you agree with me?

utterances.speaker: WILLIAM TOMLJANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes -- I'm sorry I misunderstood you earlier. I was focussing too much at the end of the -- of the paragraph. It also -- well, it's hard to say how universally this can be applied because what they're saying here is that all units from December 1st onwards which are commanded by the VP administration, implying that not all were before that date, but it doesn't necessarily mean that some were not prior to that date. Explicitly it just says that all were subordinated from that date forward -- or are commanded by -- I'm sorry, not subordinated, but commanded by the military police administration.

utterances.speaker: MS. TOMASEGOVIC TOMIC
utterances.text: Thank you. I want to move on to another subject now. That -- the subject I'm interested in is this subject of check-points and border crossings?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Before we move on to another subject, I would like to see document -- the last number of this document is 5215. Could we see that document on the screen, please. I'd like to see the English version of that document on the screen. The last part of the number is 5215. [Trial Chamber and registrar confer].

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] As we can't see it on the screen, we'll put it on the ELMO. Witness, I'd like you to read out the part that I've marked. It starts -- the last paragraph starts with the words: "As regards crime ... " and then it continues on the next page. And when you read it out, it will also be interpreted into B/C/S. Please go ahead.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes. "As regards crime of particular state interest (war crimes), unchecked and successful work of crime officials dealing with it is obvious, considering the fact that the enemy forces of MOS /Muslim armed forces/" -- I'm sorry, in brackets, not in parenthesis, Muslim armed forces, "committed several massacres against Croatian civilians at different place in central Bosnia and Herzegovina. Processing these serious war crimes and collecting qualitative evidence is ongoing and apart from filed reports, the filing of criminal reports (as printed) against Croats in Uzdol, Doljani, and Grabovica is expected."

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Does this report refer to any procedures instituted against Croats for crimes committed in Uzdol, Doljani, and Grabovica? How do you analyse this?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Well, I'd like to take a look at some point at the B/C/S here again, because I think the reason that the translators here put "as printed" inside brackets as -- was because it wouldn't necessarily or it wouldn't at all make sentence to file criminal reports against Croats for the crimes of Uzdol -- well, perhaps -- no, for Uzdol, Doljani, and Grabovica because those were all crimes allegedly committed by ABiH forces.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. Registrar, would it be possible to see the B/C/S version of this paragraph?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] It would be possible if we had the B/C/S e-court number. I don't have it. Do you have it? If Defence counsel has the number, please inform us of the e-court number and we'll then be able to have a look at the B/C/S version.

utterances.speaker: MS. TOMASEGOVIC TOMIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] In the B/C/S version it's 00405215.

utterances.speaker: MS. TOMASEGOVIC TOMIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] P09551.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Uh-huh, yeah.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Do you have it in B/C/S now?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Previous translation continues]...

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Read out the paragraph in B/C/S.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] "In the area of crime of special state interest, war crimes, the successful work of crime officials is obvious, given that the enemy MOS forces have perpetrated a number of massacres against the civilian Croat population at a number of locations in Central Bosnia and Herzegovina. The processing of these grave war crimes and the gathering of quality evidence is a permanent process.
