And in addition to a number of reports filed, it is expected that criminal reports will be filed with regard to the Croats in Uzdol, Doljani, and Grabovica." [In English] My ...

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Very well. The French interpretation was not very good because there was something that was a little ambiguous. I'd like to know whether the last part of sentence in B/C/S means that there were complaints or reports against Croats. That concerns the three locations mentioned, Uzdol, Doljani, and Grabovica.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: It's my assumption - and I'm fairly certain about this - that this is a typo, that this was an error in this document the way it was put together. I suspect what they intended to mean was that they would be filing complaints against the persons who'd committed the crimes against Croats in Uzdol, Doljani, and Grabovica. Partly I assume that, too, because the word preceding "Croats" is nad hrvatina, upon the Croat, and I assume that if they were going to be indicting Croats - and I could be wrong about this - but I assume if they were going to be indicting Croats they would say "protiv" instead of nad; against, instead of on top of. And in these places it wouldn't make sense that you were indicting Croats for that. And in this paragraph they mention it was by members of the Muslim population against the Croats, so I assume this is a typo.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] So you're saying that the translation in English "against" doesn't correspond to the phrase, the Croats were probably victims and not the authors of these crimes. Is that the gist of what you're saying?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: That's the gist of what I'm saying based on a number of things, the context of what happened, the first part of that paragraph, and also the use of the particular word they're using here before the Croats, who would have charges filed against them. It doesn't seem the -- what would be the normal choice of words. So I'm assuming it's a typo.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Very well, because the question I was asking myself was whether any investigations had been conducted which put into question HVO Croats, and now you seem to be saying that this paragraph says that there were investigations into massacres carried out by the MOS and this concerned these three locations mentioned, but apparently the Croats were victims in those locations. That's what you're saying.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, yes, that's exactly what I'm saying.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I'll give the floor back to the Defence now.

utterances.speaker: MS. TOMASEGOVIC TOMIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Your Honour. For the sake of the transcript I'd just like to check something with regard to the paragraph --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I'd like to get my document back, please.

utterances.speaker: MS. TOMASEGOVIC TOMIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] The paragraph is part of the report on the work of the HVO for the period July-December 1993, the specific paragraph is in the part entitled "the crime police sector."

utterances.speaker: MS. TOMASEGOVIC TOMIC
utterances.text: And now just tell me whether it would be correct to say that this crime police sector was a part of the Department of Internal Affairs?

utterances.speaker: WILLIAM TOMLJANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: That depends on which part of the report we're talking about. There was a criminal police sector for both the military police and for the internal affairs department, and if it's in the part of the report dealing with the ministry -- or the Department of Internal Affairs, then it would be.

utterances.speaker: MS. TOMASEGOVIC TOMIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] If necessary, but I think it may not be because Their Honours have the hard copy before them and can check that what I said about the titles is correct, perhaps I can show the witness the B/C/S version. Could we have the B/C/S version for identification. The ERN is 00405214, and then a page later just for the sake of identifying the paragraph, paragraph 2, here it is, and I would now like to go back to page 00405210.

utterances.speaker: MS. TOMASEGOVIC TOMIC
utterances.text: Can we establish that this concerns the criminal police sector within the Department of Internal Affairs?

utterances.speaker: WILLIAM TOMLJANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, if the order of pages is what you're saying, yes, we could.

utterances.speaker: MS. TOMASEGOVIC TOMIC
utterances.text: Very well. Thank you, Mr. Tomljanovich. I would now like to move on to control of traffic and border crossings. In your report you dealt with several documents, and I'll put a few brief questions to you from which it will become evident who controlled traffic and in what way in 1992 and 1993. According to my understanding of your report and the documents cited, I conclude that traffic control and check-point control was dealt with simultaneously by the military police, the civil police, the border police, the SIS, and the customs service when it comes to checking goods. Am I correct?

utterances.speaker: WILLIAM TOMLJANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I believe all of them had some role in controlling the borders, although exactly who was supposed to be doing what is beyond the scope of what I was looking into.

utterances.speaker: MS. TOMASEGOVIC TOMIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Well, to jog our memories, could we have on e-court document P00128 again, it's again the report on the work of the HVO for 1992. In the B/C/S version it's on page 11. I'll read the last paragraph in the B/C/S version. Can we have the English version shown at the same time. Well, in B/C/S it says, and this is in the section dealing with the work of the military police, it says: "Border crossings and check-points of the military police have been established at major communications and those leading towards the battle- front. Control of all military and other convoys is being carried out which are surreptitiously transporting military equipment."

utterances.speaker: MS. TOMASEGOVIC TOMIC
utterances.text: Would you agree with me that what I have read out describes the activity of the military police in connection with control of traffic, it describes what the military police does as opposed to the other bodies we have mentioned?

utterances.speaker: WILLIAM TOMLJANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, and not simply in regard to the borders but also in regard to check-points before the front -- actually, now that I see this here again and look at the translation, I don't -- yes, no, it's both, yes. Sorry.

utterances.speaker: MS. TOMASEGOVIC TOMIC
utterances.text: Would you agree with me that the same powers that the military police had with regard to traffic control also obtained in 1993?

utterances.speaker: WILLIAM TOMLJANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. In the absence of any other evidence saying otherwise, yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. TOMASEGOVIC TOMIC
utterances.text: And now I would like to move on to my last line of questioning.

utterances.speaker: MS. TOMASEGOVIC TOMIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Could we have on e-court again P04699. It's a report referring to the period from January to June, and it's 25 in B/C/S and page 16 in English. In English it's on page 16 and B/C/S it's 25.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: The year is 1993, interpreter's correction.

utterances.speaker: MS. TOMASEGOVIC TOMIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Let me read the second passage in become. It's line 5. This is a report by the military police. "A large number of prisoners is being taken to work, which makes it impossible for them to escape. There have been several such instances, but there is no possibility of increasing the number of military policemen. Prisoners are being processed by employees of the SIS and the crime prevention service."

utterances.speaker: MS. TOMASEGOVIC TOMIC
utterances.text: In view of this, would I be correct in concluding that in connection with Heliodrom because it's the only place you have mentioned so far, the criminal processing of prisoners was done not just by military policemen but also by the SIS and the criminal service?

utterances.speaker: WILLIAM TOMLJANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, although with -- I believe I mentioned Gabela as well and not just the Heliodrom, but in general I do know that the SIS had a role in processing prisoners and have seen documents to that effect.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE TRECHSEL
utterances.text: Could you please explain what the verb "processing" means in this context.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Well, I'm not entirely sure what it does mean in this context. What I would understand it to mean, based on the fact I've seen records of SIS officers going into the camps and taking statements from prisoners, that it would be in regards to their bureaucratic processing. What exactly that would entail, I'm not sure from this context. But I do know that the SIS agents did have a role in dealing with these prisoners, and I also seem to remember that generally speaking before somebody could be released, the SIS would also have to give its say-so that they had no reason to want to keep that person in detention.

utterances.speaker: MS. TOMASEGOVIC TOMIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MS. TOMASEGOVIC TOMIC
utterances.text: I'll go on reading from the same paragraph where it says: "Prison governors have been appointed who undertake all coordination work. The military police have the task of providing security for prisoners. The phenomenon of forced entry and violent investigation by certain commanders has been registered. Such behaviour should be definitely prohibited and prevented." Is it correct to conclude from the paragraph we have just read that the military police had too few employees, that it was in charge of providing security for these prisoners, and that because of this it was able to conduct a criminal investigation processing only in part.

utterances.speaker: WILLIAM TOMLJANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, no, I believe the - well, that, amongst many other things. It also mentions that where the shortage of military policemen is mentioned is in connection with of prisoners who have been taken out to work escaping, and then later in the paragraph it mentions that, you know, people coming in and forcibly -- taking prisoners and forcibly conducting an investigation with them should be stopped, but you could imply that that's because of the shortage of military police. But I don't know if everything that's mentioned in that paragraph can be attributed solely to the -- is being attributed to the shortage of military police, although that would certainly be a reasonable inference.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Can you please read out the last sentence again because it's very important for us and we need to be extremely precise, extremely accurate. Can you please read out again the last sentence, read out, please, for the interpreters to be able to translate.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes. In Croatian or -- in the Croatian original?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] In the English version.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: In the English version, the last sentence of that paragraph reads: "Such behaviour should be definitively prohibited and prevented."

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Such behaviour, I suppose it relates to the preceding sentence. Can you read the sentence just before that one?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes. The sentence before that reads: "The phenomenon of forced entry and violent investigation by certain commanders has been registered." For that sentence.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] The interpreters in the French booth tell me that "forced entry" should be replaced in French by "intrusion," there seem to be two behaviour, forced entry by elements coming from the outside and investigations conducted by, in English, "commanders" but then we should look what the term is in B/C/S, it might be the officers or the prison wardens. So we are faced with two different types of incidents. How do you analyse this? What conclusions did you draw from this?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Well, it was my understanding reading this and perhaps we should just read the B/C/S again directly for a French translation, but it's my understanding from the context here that the commanders certain -- the certain commanders who are conducting investigations forcibly are coming in from the outside as well. Because if it was the camp director, he'd be a ravnate [phoen] or another word mean being director and probably not zapoljetnik [phoen] but it was my understanding that the commanders are commanders coming from outside as well.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] So the sentence could be read differently. There can be two types of incidents, people coming from the outside who enter the premises of the prison, and then investigations conducted by commanders. But what you seem to be saying is that the investigations are conducted by the commanders in a forceful manner. In other words, the commanders mentioned here are officers coming from the outside who come inside in order to conduct investigations within the premises of the prison. That's how you understand the sentence, isn't it?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, that's how I read the sentence and I came to that conclusion because the word "forcible" is repeated twice in the B/C/S original. It's forcible entry and forcible conducting of investigations. So both are forcible, and that's exactly how I read the sentence.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE TRECHSEL
utterances.text: Could one translate "forcible investigation" into "investigation under ill treatment"?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I assumed when I read this that that was a euphemism for that, that they weren't really conducting investigations.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE TRECHSEL
utterances.text: What puzzles me, I must say, is the term "commander" here because I -- it sort of does not sound convincing that commanders in the main sense that we had the word earlier today would go and personally beat up prisoners for some investigation purposes.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Well, I think such things did happen in the camps. I've certainly seen witness statements to that effect, although I don't -- aside from this I've never seen it being attributed to investigations purposes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Very well. Please proceed, Madam.

utterances.speaker: MS. TOMASEGOVIC TOMIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] My last question -- could we have on e-court document P02533? It's a report on the work of the Office For Displaced Persons and Refugees of the 27th of July, 1993, and in the paragraph before the last in the B/C/S version, the last few lines, it reads as follows: "We have secured considerable quantities of the most varied kinds of humanitarian aid, several thousand tons. And owing to this we have managed to secure normal conditions for about 2.000 persons to live on the Heliodrom without the help of other organisations."

utterances.speaker: MS. TOMASEGOVIC TOMIC
utterances.text: What I'm interested in is whether one can conclude from this that the Office for Displaced Persons and Refugees was tasked with supplying the Heliodrom with food, medicines, and other basic necessities.

utterances.speaker: WILLIAM TOMLJANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, it's left open here. They talk in this quote that they're doing this along with other organisations and institutions. So certainly they were one of the institutions involved in doing so, although it doesn't make specific reference to what it was that authorised them to specifically provide food to the Heliodrom or who authorised them to do so. Or, I'm sorry, I'm looking at the wrong sentence. It says that they did secure materials and food for those 2.000 persons at the Heliodrom without the help of other organisations, although it doesn't say who it was who told them to do that or if this was part of their normal operation or not. Whether or not this was the sort of thing that -- one of their regular duties, I mean to say.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] This sentence does not mean that the humanitarian organisations who supplied thousands of tons of aid for the 150.000 displaced persons, that's what we read, and -- because then to supply necessities, basic necessities, for 2.000 people at the Heliodrom meant that there was no need to resort to other sources because there was already enough aid for 150.000 people. Is that the meaning of this sentence?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Well, it's the sentence prior that states in general they've accommodated for 150.000 people and that they've -- and then in addition it's the next sentence which talks about securing food and material for persons at the Heliodrom. I take it that the Heliodrom, in providing food and the proper conditions for the 2.000 people there, is just one part of everything they've done. Now, the next sentence when they say that during the collection of humanitarian aid, well I don't think we got to that question -- we didn't get to that sentence yet. But those two sentences, that's the relationship. The provision of material for the Heliodrom is one example of how they've been providing for these 150.000 people.

utterances.speaker: MS. TOMASEGOVIC TOMIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Your Honours. Thank you, Mr. Tomljanovich. I have no further questions. I don't know whether Mr. Coric has a few technical questions.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED CORIC
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED CORIC
utterances.text: Mr. Tomljanovich, my name is Valentin Coric, accused. I would like to attempt to clarify some issues with you which I believe remain unclear after this examination. I will first use a document I cannot show, but I will use only a small portion of the text. The 26th of December, 1992 -- on the 26th of December, 1992, a new organisation of the military police of the HVO took place. The document I am holding in my hands is a document issued by the Department of Defence, and it was signed on the right-hand side by the head of the department, Bruno Stojic, and on the left-hand side by the chief of the military police administration, Valentin Coric. It's an OTP document. I can read out the number, although I don't think it's necessary. One of the most frequently mentioned questions which you also pointed to today or issues is the issue of delineating responsibility between the military police and the HVO. I ask for your patience and we will comment later. I will read out two sentences which state clearly the crux of the matter. I quote: "As regards the delineation of responsibilities within the military police, the brigade military police -- polices are in charge of securing barracks and headquarters, command headquarters, securing military transports for the brigade, securing entry to the battle-field in the area of responsibility of the brigade, bringing in and detaining for the brigade," this refers to soldiers belonging to the brigade. And then another category in the military police is mentioned. "Other units, the 2nd, 3rd, 4th, and 5th Battalion of the military police are in charge of all military police work in the operative zones. Every operative zone had a military police battalion. The 1st Military Police Battalion, that's an extra battalion, is linked directly to the military police administration (the chief) and carries out, according to orders, its activities on the entire territory of the Croatian community of Herceg-Bosna." And then there's a sentence unifying all this. "The military police administration shall command and control all military police units." And the final part, the concluding part: "The commanders of military police battalions attached to the operative zones," and that refers to 2, 3, 4, and 5, "in their daily performance of tasks are directly subordinated to the commander of the operative zone and shall carry out all commands relating to the performance of military police tasks and are in accordance with the powers and competences of the military police." And the last sentence reads as follows: "Military police platoons attached to the brigade," this refers to the brigade police, "shall carry out the orders of the brigade commander within the sphere of their competence." That is the end of this text which contains a more extensive explanation. As I personally created this text at the time, I was one of its authors, and it was accepted at the defence department meeting of department heads and it was implemented in practice and the implementation continued in July and also assault battalions were added, the status of which was defined, in my view these -- this issue which has been arising for years before this Tribunal concerning lack of clarity, vagueness, and so on in the organisation of the military police, I think if -- would you agree with me that this vagueness is actually being manufactured according to the needs of a particular trial? Because this organisation here is confirmed by thousands of reports that this Tribunal has, speaking about the daily activities of the military police. Do you agree with what I say?

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: I'm going to object, Your Honour. For one thing, we've had a five-minute or a five- or ten-minute question. I don't know it's gone beyond the screen. I can't understand why we can't have a reference to a document. Why are we referring to a document that no one knows what it is. It's not clear to me why this is the case. I'd like to see the document, please.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. Coric, what is the number of the document?

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED CORIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] It's 01032246. As far as I can see, it's from the Zagreb state archives. It has a little stamp on it.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED CORIC
utterances.text: Mr. Tomljanovich, could you please answer my question --

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: I'm sorry, I object to the procedure. Why couldn't we have been told this at the very beginning rather than sitting here and listening to the document being read instead of having it in front of us. The procedure should be that if the accused themselves are going to put questions to the witness, Your Honour, notwithstanding the fact that they may be laypersons, they have to follow the procedure. So I object to this manner of proceeding.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. Scott, I don't agree with you for the following reason: An expert witness was examined by you and by Defence counsel with regard to the military police. One of the accused presents a document, he provides us with a number, but it's not a Prosecution number, apparently it's a number that concerns archival documents from Zagreb. It seems that this document establishes a distinction within the military police between five battalions. There's military police battalion 1, which has to do with the military police leadership, battalion number 1, as far as I have understood, is responsible for security, a very general term, whereas battalions 2, 3, 4, and 5 of the military police are attached to the brigade command. That's what I have understood on the basis of this document. What's important for us is for the witness to answer the question. Was he familiar with this document and what does he think about the manner in which responsibility was divided within the military police itself?

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: Your Honour, the Court misunderstands my objection. My objection was not so much as this point to the question but to the manner in which the document was put. Mr. Coric, for some reason, stood up and said he couldn't give the source of the document, he couldn't identified the document, but to read from it for some period of time. Then when I raised the issue, he gave us a number. A document should be identified by exhibit number and by number when it's first put.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Very well. This document has been identified. It's in the e-court system. Has it been registered in the e-court system? Because I'm told that the ERN number is not sufficient. What is this document's number?

utterances.speaker: MS. TOMASEGOVIC TOMIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] It's a Prosecution document, P00957.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] We could perhaps have a look at the document on the screen. So we have the document now. Witness, what would your answer be to Mr. Coric's question? According to what I have understood, the question concerned the fact that the 1st Battalion was under the military police leadership, whereas the other four battalions were under the brigade commands. What is your response?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Well, I should first of all say that my response is based on things I've seen prior to working on this report. In this report it was not my intention to get into this whole issue or to deal with the military police and issues of command and control in this detail. I do know, however, from other things I've seen that the basic idea was that these various police -- military police battalions were sent out into the operational zones. And while they were in those operational zones for the matter of day-to-day military commands, they were under the control of their operational zone commanders. Now, I don't know and I'm not sure if this document or other documents make it entirely clear, in the event of a disciplinary problem involving soldiers in those military police battalions, whether or not processing the disciplinary -- any disciplinary or criminal proceedings against members of those units would be primarily the responsibility of the operational zone commander or of the head of the military police administration. And that's not a question I was intending to get into, but I do know some things from it from prior cases.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE TRECHSEL
utterances.text: I think perhaps the question Mr. Coric has asked was slightly different. You have at one point this afternoon said that the delineation of competencies of the military police and other authorities was very difficult and complicated a matter, whereas I think Mr. Coric is putting to you that it is something very simple according to the document. Is that -- did I interpret you correctly, Mr. Coric?

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED CORIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, perfectly.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Well, if that's the case, I can only say that people who are supposed to be more well-versed in these issues than I am seem to think it's not a simple problem. And if it was as simple as looking at the one document, it's a shame the one document wasn't introduced by Mr. Coric and others in prior cases if it does answer all the questions, which I wouldn't be in a position to know.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Let's take a specific case. Let's take a given operative zone, operative zone X. There are check- points in this operative zone because such question was put. The check- points are there to provide security. According to what we have been told, this would be the responsibility of the 1st Battalion. In the operative zone, if any individuals arrested by the police and taken to prison Y, for example, in such a case would this be the responsibility of the leader in the operative zone, the brigade commander, and the leadership of the military police, that is -- has responsibility of the 1st Battalion doesn't necessarily have to be aware of the matter, they are not necessarily responsible. That's the problem. How would you analyse this? What would your response be?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Well, I would say again that first of all this is outside the scope of what I was intending to deal with --

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: And I'm going to intervene there, Your Honour. I don't know how many more times I have to say this. We keep putting questions to this witness that are beyond the scope of what he was asked to do. So we can continue to do that and ask for this witness to speculate, but this witness was never asked to look at the military -- the operations, the detailed operations of the military police. And when we looked at various charts, including the organisational charts, the witness has said a number of times that he didn't make the charts on the bottom half of the page and so I object myself because we're now going -- repeatedly made this point, so we keep putting questions to this witness that are beyond the scope of what he was asked to do, so it's pure speculation. The witness is not qualified. He hasn't looked at it and he shouldn't speculate about it.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Witness, you've heard the answer as suggested to you by the Prosecution, according to whom, you are not competent to answer such questions. Or do you believe that you are competent?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: No. If it gets into questions of the day-to-day operation of the armed forces and the military police, then I am not. If it's just where the military police fits within the department and where they're mentioned in broader references to broader structures and processes, then I would be competent. But something like this that gets into day-to-day operation, I would not be.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. TOMASEGOVIC TOMIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I'd just like to add something. This document is called "The structure of the HVO military police," Mr. Tomljanovich, and your report was entitled "The governing bodies and organs." I think this is an important subject for your report. Since this is a Prosecution document, I'd like to know whether when drafting your report you had access to this document. Have you seen this document before in fact?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Well, I'll answer -- there's a few questions there. I'll answer them in order. First of all, it was my charge to deal with the political and governing structures and processing, not the military structures and processes. For example, if an order said: The structure of the 3rd Platoon in whatever place in Vitez, that wouldn't make it subject to my report. So I would not understand this particular order to be part of the sphere of things I was supposed to be addressing in my report. Now, to the rest of your question, this question -- this document here, just looking at the ERNs on the translation and on the original -- if we could scroll up to the top of the original. Yeah. This is the sort of document I would have had access to. Now, I have all -- access to all sorts of things, but they're not necessarily things I would be looking for. I think in this instance this is something where, if I'd been told to look at it, I would have been able to find it, but it wasn't the sort of thing I was looking for in drafting my report because it gets down to a level of detail beyond the sorts of things I was intending to deal with.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Your Honour, I'm just not quite sure that the answer -- that he answered the question. Did he look at this document? And if so, we know why he didn't put it in his report, but I would like to know: Was he aware of the existence of this document? He's the expert. There is a section on the military, there's a section covering the military police. Obviously as the expert, he decides what he's going to include and/or exclude in his report. The question is: Was he aware of the document? Did he know the document -- of the document's existence? Had he read it? It's a yes, no, maybe, I can't remember, you know, the choices are few.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Have you seen this document? And if so, why didn't you refer to it in your report?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Well, few reasons. First of all, I may have seen this document years ago when we initially went to the archives and found these documents. That's conceivable, but I would not have seen it since then, nor do I remember having seen it, nor have I had a chance to read through this beginning to end yet here either. So I might not have ever read this document. This document and other documents, as far as I understand -- now, this is still -- remember a document I have not read beginning to end, is a document which I assume, based on Mr. Coric's characterisation of it, a document which would deal with command and control issues inside the military police, which I would have, had I known about it, I would have thought that this was something that was a military problem which should be dealt with by the military expert, which the Prosecution intends to call. However, as I was writing my report, I did not know specifically about the existence of this document.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Mr. President, I don't want to take up --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. Karnavas, we've understood --

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: [Previous translation continues]...

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] -- the answer. We should leave -- we should allow Mr. Coric to continue.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Absolutely. I was going to point out the de jure part because it's part of his report.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. Coric.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED CORIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED CORIC
utterances.text: Mr. Tomljanovich, when preparing for the report you drafted, did you come across any other documents that were drafted on the basis of this one and define the role of command for the military police? There were scores of them from the very highest level to the lowest level. Did you ever come across a single such document that referred to the same subject I have been discussing now, yes or no?

utterances.speaker: WILLIAM TOMLJANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I may have earlier but not in preparation of this report, not with these particular issues, no.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED CORIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Mr. Tomljanovich. I have no further questions. Thank you, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Very well. Mr. Coric's Defence has concluded its cross-examination. We have another 25 minutes before we adjourn. Who will start now? We do have 25 minutes, so obviously we won't have time to conclude with the cross-examination. Mr. Scott, I'm turning to you now because next week I see that you have planned for a number of witnesses who will be appearing here. The Judges have discussed this. It would be good if the cross-examination could continue very rapidly and not one month or two months later. If the witness could come on Monday again so that the cross-examination can be completed, so on Monday, the 18th of September, in -- well, in that case it would be necessary to have the other witnesses appearing a little later. Is that possible or not?

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: I don't know, Your Honour. I'd have to check with Mr. Mundis and check on scheduling. If the witnesses have already arranged their travel and are coming it may not be possible to change it at this point since Mr. -- we, too, are anxious to conclude Mr. Tomljanovich's testimony, as he is, so he can go on with his life without this hanging over his head. But I don't know what the schedule is in terms of whether people are coming from a great distance, and it -- unfortunately for Mr. Tomljanovich, since he is here in The Hague, it is easier for him to fit in on the available time spots, than it is to cancel people coming from a long distance.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] There are three reasons in favour of continuing with his cross-examination next Monday. Firstly, since he has taken the solemn declaration and he must avoid any form of contact with the Prosecution, this constitutes a technical problem if he remains in such a situation for a month, that might be difficult; and then secondly, the Defence teams that have yet to cross-examine the witness must have prepared their questions. If we postpone his testimony, this will make things more difficult. And then if we return in a few weeks' time, it will be necessary to take things up where we left off, to start all over again. So see about this with Mr. Mundis, but it would be ideal if he could come back on Monday and we'd have the other witnesses at a later -- the witness who was supposed to appear on Monday would appear on Tuesday instead. So this concerns the week that commences on the 18th and finishes on the 22nd. Discuss the matter with Mr. Mundis, but I've just provided you with three reasons for which it would be good to call the witness back on Monday. We have another witness tomorrow and the day after, and Thursday it's not possible. I'll now give the floor to Pusic's Defence counsel.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAHOTA
utterances.text: We started the session at 5.20 and I understand this session is to be of 90 minutes' duration. I have approximately between half an hour and 45 minutes of questions, and I would like to ask the Tribunal if they would wish me to begin now with the prospect that I may not finish and resume next week or alternatively if the Tribunal is of the view that I may be allowed to resume next Monday when this witness returns.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Ideally you would start now because we have 25 precious minutes remaining, and then next Monday, if possible, you will complete your cross-examination. Perhaps there are some questions which are more important, others that are less important. Perhaps you could deal with the important questions next time and deal with the secondary questions now. I don't know. It's for you to decide. We have another 25 minutes and it would be useful if you started now.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAHOTA
utterances.text: Mr. Tomljanovich, my name is Roger Sahota. I am the co-counsel for Mr. Pusic. I would like to ask you a few questions in regard to your testimony and your report insofar as it relates to my client. I would like to ask you to begin by turning to appendices B and C of your report found at pages 123 and 127 of the English language version. Appendix B is entitled "members of the HVO HZ-HB and other attendees" and appendix C is a list of HR-HB government members as of February 1993. Could you clarify, is it correct that Mr. Pusic never held the post of minister or deputy minister within the HVO HZ-HB cabinet or its various incarnations; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: WILLIAM TOMLJANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, he was never a minister nor a department head.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAHOTA
utterances.text: Did he hold the post of assistant department head?

utterances.speaker: WILLIAM TOMLJANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, he did not as far as I am aware.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAHOTA
utterances.text: Mr. Tomljanovich, is it correct to state that Mr. Pusic is not mentioned at all within either appendix B or C of your report?

utterances.speaker: WILLIAM TOMLJANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, that would be fair to say.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAHOTA
utterances.text: I'd like you to turn now to appendix E of your report which can be found at page 129. My first question is this: Is it correct to say that cabinet meetings of the HVO HZ-HB and its various successors were not just restricted to cabinet members; other interested individuals could attend?

utterances.speaker: WILLIAM TOMLJANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: They could and did attend.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAHOTA
utterances.text: Turning to appendix E, during the time-frame that you have logged the attendance of individuals at cabinet meetings, is it correct to say that Mr. Pusic has only been recorded as having attended one cabinet meeting between 1992 and 1993?

utterances.speaker: WILLIAM TOMLJANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I believe that's correct if you're referring to the 21st of September, 1993. That's the only one I can think of off the top of my head and that I see here.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAHOTA
utterances.text: Thank you. I would like to turn now to the issue of exchange of prisoners and displaced persons and would ask you and the Court to refer to pages 61 and 62 of your report. Now, we have heard evidence that Mr. Pusic was appointed head of the service for the exchange of prisoners on the 5th of July, 1993. Is that correct?

utterances.speaker: WILLIAM TOMLJANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. Its full title was the service for the exchange of prisoners and other persons, but yes it is that date, July 5th, 1993.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAHOTA
utterances.text: Would you agree this was not the first body empowered to deal this particular issue?

utterances.speaker: WILLIAM TOMLJANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I'm sure it wasn't the first body to deal with this.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAHOTA
utterances.text: And on paragraph 158 of your report, you refer to the existence of the commission for the exchange of prisoners, which in itself is referred to in the notes of a cabinet meeting dated the 17th of December, 2002. Is that right?

utterances.speaker: WILLIAM TOMLJANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I do.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAHOTA
utterances.text: [Microphone not activated]?

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Microphone, please.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Oh, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAHOTA
utterances.text: Could you turn now to paragraph 160 of your report you begin by saying: "The multitude of groups exchanged in exchanges presented problems."

utterances.speaker: WILLIAM TOMLJANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I do.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAHOTA
utterances.text: Is it fair then to say that by the early part of 1993, that prisoners exchanges were being dealt with not just by the commission for the exchange of prisoners; there were lots of bodies involved?

utterances.speaker: WILLIAM TOMLJANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, and I based what I said there on the minutes of the 30th Session of the HVO, which I cite below. And, yes, I think there were also various local bodies that were involved that have been made reference to in these meetings.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAHOTA
utterances.text: You referred -- you used the phrase "multitude of groups." One of the groups involved also included the office for the refugees, exiled and displaced persons, which you referred to using the initials ODPR. Would you agree with that?

utterances.speaker: WILLIAM TOMLJANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I believe they were charged with some role in this as well.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAHOTA
utterances.text: Thank you. I'd just like to turn quickly to the issue of detention units, which you deal with in pages 93 to 101 of your report. The first mention you make of my client in this section is at paragraph 261. You refer to the notes of a cabinet meeting on the 19th of July --

utterances.speaker: WILLIAM TOMLJANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAHOTA
utterances.text: -- where a decision was made for a three-man delegation to visit the facility at Capljina.

utterances.speaker: WILLIAM TOMLJANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, and I believe it was facilities, not just facility at Capljina, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAHOTA
utterances.text: Thank you. Mr. Pusic was one of that delegation. Is that correct?

utterances.speaker: WILLIAM TOMLJANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I believe he was -- yes, he was. Yes, he was, definitely.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAHOTA
utterances.text: Is it also correct that the following day after the inspection had taken place, one member of the delegation reported back to the next cabinet meeting on the 20th of July?

utterances.speaker: WILLIAM TOMLJANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I am sure they reported back. I don't know which one of the members it was off the top of my head who was responsible for doing so, but they did respond the next day.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAHOTA
utterances.text: Turning to appendix E of your report, it would appear that Mr. Pusic did not attend the cabinet meeting of the 20th of July. Could you verify that, please?

utterances.speaker: WILLIAM TOMLJANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, just a second, although the definitive answer to that wouldn't be my appendix, it would be the minutes of the meeting itself. I may have made a mistake in transcribing -- in marking down who was present. Now, let me check here. This is the 20th of July, and no, he's not listed as being present, at least not in my appendix for that date.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAHOTA
utterances.text: Mr. Tomljanovich, I can assure you that I've read the notes for that meeting and I can assure you that Mr. Pusic is not listed under those attending, however due to lack of time I can't put the document to you. I can put to you the suggestion that it was actually Mr. Buntic who was also part of the delegation that reported back to the cabinet?

utterances.speaker: WILLIAM TOMLJANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: That certainly would make sense since he was a department head and was attending these meetings regularly in any event.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAHOTA
utterances.text: And can I also ask you to accept, Mr. Tomljanovich, my assertion that there is no mention of Mr. Pusic at all in the cabinet meeting notes of the 20th of July? Again, I don't -- for lack of time, I don't have the opportunity to put the document to you, but you will have the opportunity to examine it after.

utterances.speaker: WILLIAM TOMLJANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: If he's not in the document, he's not in the document, and anything I know about that meeting is only based on the document.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAHOTA
utterances.text: Now, the commission which we've heard so much about was set up on the 6th of September. Is it correct to say by then, as you said when you were giving evidence on the 6th of August before this Court -- 6th of September before this Court, that no senior HVO official or body was taking responsibility for the conditions within the detention camps. Is that a fair characterisation of the general context in which the commission's established?

utterances.speaker: WILLIAM TOMLJANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. Very quickly I think you're talking about the commission which was created on 6th of August I referred to in my testimony in 6th of September. But yes, in the sense that nobody stood up and said: This is my job and I'm responsible for fixing all of these things. Individuals took individual actions, but nobody stood up to claim responsibility for the conditions.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAHOTA
utterances.text: And in paragraph 265 of your report, you describe this purported commission as having the sweeping power to take charge of all detention units and prisons in which prisoners of war and military detainees are held. Is that correct?

utterances.speaker: WILLIAM TOMLJANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, that's what it says in the order.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAHOTA
utterances.text: I'd like now to examine some of the events that took place shortly after the commission was set up on the 6th of August. A few days later, there was a cabinet meeting that takes place on the 11th of August, and that is followed by another cabinet meeting on the 18th of August. There is a reference to both these meetings at paragraph 266 of your report. Again, an examination of appendix E confirms that Mr. Pusic was not present at either meeting. Would you agree with that?

utterances.speaker: WILLIAM TOMLJANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I'll take your word for it. And if he's not in the -- if he's not in the document, he's not in the document, and that's I know what is in that particular document, but I would not be surprised were he not there.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAHOTA
utterances.text: Well, Mr. Tomljanovich, I would also ask you to take my word for this. I read through the notes of both those meetings and there was no reference to either Mr. Pusic or the commission. Can I put that to you?

utterances.speaker: WILLIAM TOMLJANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't recall any mention, so that would not surprise me.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAHOTA
utterances.text: And again there is no mention of Mr. Pusic or the commission, despite the fact that at the end of the extract at paragraph 266, despite the fact that at the meeting it was discussed that departments should be tasked with organising special military and civilian prisons in keeping with HZ HB regulations and international conventions. So despite that discussion, there was no mention of Mr. Pusic and the commission. Does that surprise you?

utterances.speaker: WILLIAM TOMLJANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, no mention in the minutes. It is somewhat surprising, although quite a lot of the things which all of these persons were doing in this period seems to be surprising, but that's what's in the documents.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAHOTA
utterances.text: Could you turn now please to paragraph 268 of your report, it's on the next page. This refers to a meeting that took place on the 2nd of September, which we've heard a great deal about already in the course of your testimony. Again, can you recall whether Mr. Pusic was attend -- was present during that meeting?

utterances.speaker: WILLIAM TOMLJANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't believe he was and I don't believe he should have been because it would have only been the defence minister with his assistants and the deputy defence minister, and I do not recall him being there. I would have been surprised had he been there.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAHOTA
utterances.text: I'd like to ask you to look again briefly at appendix E. As you pointed out earlier, the only reference to Mr. Pusic ever having attended a cabinet meeting relates to the meeting that took place on the 21st of September?

utterances.speaker: WILLIAM TOMLJANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAHOTA
utterances.text: Again, Mr. Tomljanovich, time pressures, I'm going to ask you to take it from me that I've checked the notes of that meeting. Although Mr. Pusic was present, there's no reference in that his name isn't mentioned and there's no reference to the commission in the notes of that meeting. Would you agree with that?

utterances.speaker: WILLIAM TOMLJANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, do you mean that he was listed as being present but he's not listed as saying anything specific inside it but he is mentioned as being present at the --

utterances.speaker: MR. SAHOTA
utterances.text: Exactly --

utterances.speaker: WILLIAM TOMLJANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: -- header of the list.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAHOTA
utterances.text: And there's no mention of the commission?

utterances.speaker: WILLIAM TOMLJANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: That's entirely possible.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAHOTA
utterances.text: Last Wednesday when you gave evidence, you were asked by the President whether the director or wardens of any prisons or detention facilities will have to follow the orders and instructions of the purported commission, and you answered words to the effect that they wouldn't necessarily be subordinate to the members of the commission in the hierarchical structure. Do you agree with that?

utterances.speaker: WILLIAM TOMLJANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, because the -- that particular order is not specific about that. It says that they have to follow any orders or instructions that are given by members of the commission, but it doesn't necessarily change -- change the structure. You can be ordered by one superior to follow an order by somebody else that he designates without changing the general structure, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAHOTA
utterances.text: I just want to concentrate briefly on this topic of orders and instructions emanating from the purported commission. You said earlier in your testimony that you'd spent a great deal of space - and I would also speculate time - working on your report, studying the handling of prisoners. Is that correct?

utterances.speaker: WILLIAM TOMLJANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Quite a bit of time, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAHOTA
utterances.text: Is it correct to say that there is no mention in your report of any orders, of any reports emanating from the purported commission set up on the 6th of August?

utterances.speaker: WILLIAM TOMLJANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, and I should add that I can only provide evidence from archival collections to which we have access. I've never seen any collection of documents coming from that -- from the service that Mr. Pusic headed.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAHOTA
utterances.text: And the commission?

utterances.speaker: WILLIAM TOMLJANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Neither from the commission. I've never seen a collection of documents from the commission.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAHOTA
utterances.text: So just to be clear about this. You've searched the archives and you've never come across any documents pertaining either to the service or the commission?

utterances.speaker: WILLIAM TOMLJANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, I wouldn't go that far, no. They are mentioned in other documents, as indeed they're mentioned in a number of places in this report. What I meant to say was the sorts of collections we've had access to, we don't have the incoming and outcoming mail from other the commission or the service, although they are referred to elsewhere.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAHOTA
utterances.text: You can't rule out the possibility, though, can you, Mr. Tomljanovich, that the reason you couldn't find any of this documentation was that it simply didn't exist?

utterances.speaker: WILLIAM TOMLJANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I would be very surprised if a service and a commission had been established and didn't produce paper. The one thing that amazes me with everything I've seen in the archives is how much paper every office produces. So I would be very surprised if there was nothing.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAHOTA
utterances.text: But if the commission was created in paper only, then it wouldn't be surprising, would it, if it never had any practical influence or effect, then it wouldn't be surprising?

utterances.speaker: WILLIAM TOMLJANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, the less it did and the fewer employees, then indeed the less there would be to find, but that doesn't mean it's not there or might not be there -- or might not be there as well. You just don't know. I can only speak from what I have evidence from.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAHOTA
utterances.text: Well, Mr. Tomljanovich, I think my time is up. Thank you very much.

utterances.speaker: WILLIAM TOMLJANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Very well. It's time to conclude. Mr. Scott.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: I'm aware of the time, but to respond to the inquiry the Court directed to the Prosecution earlier. It would assist the Prosecution a great deal if the -- in the next day or two, preferably by tomorrow, the Defence would be able to give us some sort of estimate for the cross-examinations next week. This has come up before. If we knew, had some idea, rough idea, not a specific, but a rough idea of the cross- examinations time, then we could be better to say if we would be able to fit Mr. Tomljanovich in. A number of the witnesses next week are crime- base witnesses under 89(F) and may very well be -- based on past experience that's all I'm saying that the cross-examinations may be very short. So if we could get estimates, that would assist.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] From what I understand, after the Defence of Mr. Pusic conclude, they still have 25 to 30 minutes, then Mr. Karnavas will have the floor with the time that was given to him by Mr. Praljak and -- unless I'm mistaken about the amount of time left to you, Mr. Sahota.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAHOTA
utterances.text: If I may assist, Mr. President. It's unlikely that I will require any more time. I will review my notes, but if that may assist the Tribunal.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: Your Honour, I apologise. I may have been misunderstood. It wasn't so much the time for Mr. Tomljanovich, although that would assist, it was for the other witnesses scheduled for next week.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. Karnavas.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: As for the witnesses coming up next week, Your Honour, it has been our practice to be extremely laconic when it comes to crime-based witnesses. We do not expect to take up any time. There may be a question or two combined for all the witnesses, but we do not expect at this point in time. I cannot speak for my colleagues. As for Mr. Tomljanovich, of course I would like any time that wasn't used by the Pusic Defence team to also be added on, you know, for the entire amount that was allotted to us. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] If I look at the schedule you gave me, the witness who was supposed to appear on Monday was supposed to take place -- to take two hours and a half for examination-in-chief. According to the Rules the Defence would have the same time. The witness for the next day, 1.0, so I suppose that's one hour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] So I suppose you were planning to take one hour for that witness. So now if I look at the witness for Wednesday, there were two witnesses. For one of the witnesses, one hour, and the other was another witness that would take one hour. So if I look at your schedule, at your chart, it seems to me that it will probably be possible to fit in the witness we have here in the courtroom on Monday and then to hear all the other witnesses because the Defence counsel tell us that when it comes to crime-base witnesses they won't have many questions to put to them. So if you say that you will need about one hour for examination-in-chief, the Defence will probably need one hour to a maximum of one hour and a half for cross-examination. So I think it's possible for us to fit in the witness we have here today. That's why I was putting my questions to Mr. Karnavas. Mr. Karnavas, how much time do you think you will need for this witness here? You have to know it?

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Well, Your Honour, as you can see --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Apparently you've said it, but I've missed that.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: I haven't committed myself, but if I could have three days, fine; if I could have two days, that's fine; but if I can't have three or two days, whatever time is available I would like. Now, if the Court tells me I only have one day, one full day, Monday, then I will do my level best to fit it all in one day. So I think I'm being reasonable at this point in time. But realistically speaking I could spend three or four days going over the testimony of this gentleman and it would be interesting, but that's neither here nor there.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Fine, we'll do our own calculations, and as early as tomorrow we'll tell you how much time you will have. Yes, Ms. Nozica.

utterances.speaker: MS. NOZICA
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I only wish -- thank you, Your Honours. I only wish to repeat my request from the last session for additional questions after the examination of my colleague Mr. Karnavas. I need some 15 to 20 minutes to correct some serious errors, especially in errors in interpretation which would have very serious consequences. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Fine. We take note of it, and the Judges will discuss the matter. Yes, Mr. Kovacic.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOVACIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honours, I only wish you to bear in mind when deciding on the time to be taken for these four witnesses planned for next week, two of these four witnesses will be 80(F) [as interpreted] witnesses. We have never yet worked according to this pattern. So the witness may be in the witness box only half an hour, but then we have to see how much that testimony is worth timewise The witness can spend half an hour testifying, but if I have ten facts on which I have to cross-examine, it comes to the same as if the witness had testified. So I hope that a fair criterion will be used with these four witnesses because if the same criteria are used as up till now, this will not be fair for these two witnesses. I think there will be only two, although originally there were to be three of these witnesses. Also, as far as the Defence of General Praljak is concerned, we have quite a few topics to deal with in the case of two of these witnesses, but I do not wish to commit myself at this point. We can do that tomorrow if necessary.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Very well. The Judges will look at the issue of Rule 89(F), but it would be paradoxical for witnesses heard according -- under 89(F) to take longer than witnesses heard traditionally. But we'll have time to discuss the matter by the end of next week. Witness, you've understood that your testimony has now been concluded provisionally speaking, but you are still under oath. Therefore, you shall not speak with Mr. Mundis or Mr. Scott about the essence of your -- of the cross-examination, the questions put to you. But since you are a staff member of the OTP, obviously you can keep working at the OTP, but you should not discuss the essence or the subject of your cross-examination. You've understood that, I'm sure. So no need to dwell on the matter. We'll now conclude and we'll start again tomorrow at 9.00, and we hope that the service in charge of bringing the accused here won't forget them.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: to be reconvened on Tuesday, the 12th day of September, 2006, at 9.00 a.m.

procedural_notes.text: --- Whereupon the hearing adjourned at 7.10 p.m.,
